name: Oslo Opera House
label: Oslo Opera House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Langkaigata' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Langkaigata nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/810259696: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Oslo Opera House' (301 m across).
notes: Marble building where you can walk up the sloping roof for fjord views.

text.description:
The Oslo Opera House is the home of the Norwegian National Opera and Ballet. It sits in the Bjørvika neighbourhood at the head of the Oslofjord. Snøhetta designed it, and it opened on 12 April 2008. Its sloping white surfaces are covered in Carrara marble and white granite, so the whole building seems to rise straight out of the water. That clean, angled shape is what makes it so easy to photograph.

One guide suggests a quieter alternative view from Langkaigata, across the harbour, which shows the front of the building with its reflection in the water. The waterfront promenade gives you a foreground, and the same guide describes it as lined with floating saunas, which adds some local colour. It is also a quieter place to stand than the building itself.

The roof slopes down to ground level so that visitors can walk up it, which makes a good second set of pictures. From the top you get a wide view over the fjord and the Barcode towers. The two views complement each other: the reflection shot shows the building as a whole, and the roof shot shows what surrounds it.

White marble can look flat or too bright on a phone, so check the exposure before you take the picture. The reflection also looks best when the water is calm.
text.geographic_location: The Opera House is in the Bjørvika neighbourhood of central Oslo, on the waterfront at the head of the Oslofjord.
text.directions_text: There are no public transport stops listed for this spot, so head for Bjørvika in central Oslo and walk to the Langkaigata waterfront promenade. Once you are the Opera House is to the south-east, about 3 minutes on foot away. Follow the harbour edge if you want to walk over and go up onto the roof afterwards. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole front, its reflection and some of the promenade in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, more natural view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-3x), use it to pick out the marble slopes and the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Langkaigata (waterfront promenade across the harbour from the building, looking back at its front). The front of the Opera House with its reflection in the harbour water, framed by the promenade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on the lower third line, so the building and its reflection fill the frame evenly. Keep the phone level so the angled roof and the horizon look straight. For a second shot, go over to the Opera House itself and photograph the white marble slope rising out of the harbour, with the fjord and the Barcode towers behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white marble keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case ripples spoil the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon, when the sun falls on the front of the building. Calm weather gives the clearest reflection.

text.access_note: The promenade is open public space, and the Opera House roof is normally open to walk on, but sections can close for safety or maintenance and the marble may be restricted in snow or ice, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Calm water gives the clearest reflection.
White surfaces can look too bright on a phone unless the exposure is lowered.
The building's roof gives a wide view over the fjord and the Barcode towers (the Barcode towers are named in the viewpoint notes, not in the written sources).

name: Munch Museum
label: Munch Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Akershus Festning' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Akershus festning' (node/8073672181): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/545260792: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Munchmuseet' (127 m across).
notes: Tall waterfront museum with The Scream.

text.description:
The Munch Museum, marketed simply as MUNCH, is the big art museum on the Bjørvika waterfront, right beside the Oslo Opera House. It is dedicated to Edvard Munch and holds almost 28,000 artworks, which moved here from the old museum at Tøyen before the new building was opened by King Harald V on 22 October 2021. The building is tall and tilted, so it stands out clearly against the harbour and the city behind it.

From the raised ground there you look across the water, and the museum becomes a distant, modern shape on the waterfront. That distance is the point of the shot: the old stone fortress, the open harbour and the museum all sit in one frame, with the old and the new side by side.

On a phone, the museum will look small at the default lens (1x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring it closer, and keep a strip of water in the foreground so the picture has depth. If you want a different view, the Operahuset is a good second viewpoint. From there you can frame the museum's tilted tower against the Barcode high-rises and the fjord.

Take a few shots at different zoom levels. Then pick the one where the building and the harbour feel balanced.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Bjørvika, on the Oslo waterfront next to the Oslo Opera House.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to see the whole scene, then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to make the museum bigger in the frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of harbour and sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Akershus Festning. The museum seen across the harbour from the fortress grounds, with the building as a distant subject. Keep the main view over the water clear, so nothing blocks the line between you and the museum.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the museum on one of the vertical lines, with the water along the lower third. A small piece of fortress wall or a tree at the edge of the frame can add depth, as long as it does not cut across the view of the museum. For a different view, try the Operahuset, where the tilted tower can be framed against the Barcode high-rises and the fjord.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the museum to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the building does not turn into a silhouette. Hold the phone with both hands when using telephoto, as zoom makes every shake more visible.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is likely to give the best light, because the sun is then behind you and falls on the museum's face. Soft, clear light after sunrise or before sunset works well too.

text.access_note: The fortress grounds are open public grounds, but some parts of the fortress and the museum itself may have visiting rules or tickets, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From Akershus Festning the museum is roughly east, so afternoon and evening sun, from the west, should fall on the side facing the fortress.
At the default lens (1x) the museum will look small from across the harbour, so telephoto helps.
Parts of Akershus Festning and the museum may have visiting rules or tickets.

name: Viking Ship Museum
label: Viking Ship Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28475470: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Viking Ship Museum' (103 m across).
notes: Houses the Oseberg and Gokstad Viking ships on Bygdøy.

text.description: The Viking Ship Museum (Vikingskipshuset på Bygdøy) stands on the Bygdøy peninsula in Oslo and is part of the Museum of Cultural History of the University of Oslo. It was built to shelter three Viking-era burial ships, from Tune, Gokstad and Oseberg. The Oseberg ship is the best known, and it came from the largest known ship burial in the world. The building is also a story in itself. Arnstein Arneberg won the architectural contest, the Oseberg hall was ready for the ship's move in 1926, and the halls for the Gokstad and Tune ships followed in 1932. The last hall was finished in 1957, after delays that were partly due to the Second World War. The outline of the complex is about 103 m across, so it is a big, calm subject for a phone. For the best photo, step back from the entrance and let the building fill the frame, with the sky above it and a little foreground below. Keep the phone level so the long walls stay straight. Because the museum is temporarily closed from September 2021 until 2027, interior photos are not possible at present, and it is worth checking the official site for what is open and what you can see before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is on the Bygdøy peninsula in Oslo.
text.directions_text: Head for the Bygdøy peninsula in Oslo, and look for Vikingskipshuset på Bygdøy. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local journey planner for how to get there. The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so there is no walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the walls, then switch to the default lens (1x) as you step back for a calmer, truer-looking view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as rooflines and entrance features.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk back a little from the walls until the whole front fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the roof and walls with them so the building stays straight. Leave a strip of ground in the foreground for depth. If the building is too large to fit, take a panorama and move the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks too bright. Tap again if the exposure shifts when you move the phone.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a building like this. Early in the day also tends to be quieter.

text.access_note: The museum is temporarily closed until 2027, so check the official site before you go.

name: Vigeland Sculpture Park
label: Vigeland Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Monolitten' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Monolitten' (way/807822129): middle (3 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4334023: large area 'Frogner Park' (1153 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Gustav Vigeland's sculptures, including the Monolith.

text.description:
The Vigeland Sculpture Park is the part of Frogner Park, Oslo's largest park, that holds Gustav Vigeland's sculptures, bridges and fountains. Building began in 1924, and it is described as the largest sculpture park in the world made by a single artist. Most of the figures show people doing ordinary things: running, wrestling, dancing, hugging and holding hands. That makes them easy to photograph, because you can see the story in a single frame. The park is also very popular, with one to two million visitors a year, so a patient wait for a gap pays off.

The best-known spot for a phone photo is the Monolith plateau. A 17 m granite column of climbing figures rises from a circular area, and shooting up from its foot gives a strong, simple picture against the sky. Walk all the way round it, because the figures look different from each side. For a change of scene, the bronze 'angry boy' (Sinnataggen) on the bridge works well close up, or with the bridge's sculpture groups behind it. Frogner Park also has a large rose garden and many mature trees, which add colour and softer backgrounds if the sculptures feel too grey.
text.geographic_location: The park lies in the Frogner district in Oslo's West End, and it is the largest green space in the city. The sculptures sit within Frogner Park, which has the old manor house in its southern part.
text.directions_text: Head for Frogner in Oslo's West End and go in through the park. Once inside, follow the central line of sculptures up to the column. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole column in from close to its base. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out single figures near the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (from the foot of the granite column on the Monolith plateau, shooting upward). The 17 m granite column with its climbing figures rising against the sky, with the plateau's circular area in the foreground. The subject lies to the south-east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the column on a vertical line. Leave a strip of the plateau at the bottom of the frame to give a sense of scale. Walk slowly round the column and compare angles. For an alternative, try the 'angry boy' (Sinnataggen) on the bridge, close up or with the bridge's sculpture groups behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the column to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. Take a few shots, and try a Live Photo if people are drifting through the frame, so you can pick the cleanest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late evening light is best. An early weekday visit is likely to be quieter around the column.

text.access_note: Frogner Park is a public park that is open to visitors at all times; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit the Vigeland Museum or anything else with a ticket.

name: Akershus Fortress
label: Akershus Fortress
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Akershus festning' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Akershus festning' (node/8073672181): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/13931023: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Akershus castle' (126 m across).
notes: Medieval castle and fortress above the harbour.

text.description: Akershus Fortress is a medieval castle on the edge of the Oslofjord, built to protect Oslo and to serve as a royal residence. Building is thought to have begun in the late 1290s under King Haakon V. After a great fire in 1624, King Christian IV moved the city closer to the fortress, and the castle was remodelled with Italian-inspired bastions. It has survived every siege, and today it also serves as the prime minister's temporary office. That mix of thick stone walls, grassy ramparts and open water makes it easy to photograph. From the southern ramparts the walls fill the foreground, while the harbour and the Aker Brygge waterfront stretch away to the west and the fjord opens out to the south. Guides often name this walkway as the most-photographed spot on the site. Keep a stretch of wall in the bottom of the frame so the picture feels anchored, and let the water and sky fill the rest. If you want the fortress itself in the picture, Aker Brygge across the harbour basin shows it framed by the waterfront. Ekebergparken gives a wide, raised view over the city centre. Check the framing there, as it is more of a westward panorama.
text.geographic_location: The fortress stands on the Oslofjord waterfront in central Oslo, overlooking the harbour and across the water from the Aker Brygge waterfront.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Akershus Fortress on the harbour side of central Oslo. The walkway along the southern ramparts faces the harbour. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the wall, harbour and sky together, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out boats or the Aker Brygge buildings across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (southern ramparts (festningsvollene), facing the harbour). The fortress walls in the foreground, with the harbour and Aker Brygge waterfront stretching west and the fjord opening southward behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. Place a stretch of the fortress wall in the lower corner of the frame and let the harbour and Aker Brygge fill the middle, with the fjord beyond. For a view that includes the fortress itself, Aker Brygge across the harbour is an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the water or the sky, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone walls do not turn washed out. Keep your phone still for a moment before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun is in the west and lights the water.

text.access_note: The fortress grounds are free to walk, but the museum and some inner areas charge admission and side gates can close early in winter, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: An ultra-wide lens helps fit the wall, harbour and sky into one frame.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the sky's colour against bright water.

label: Kon-Tiki Museum

notes: Thor Heyerdahl's expedition rafts on Bygdøy.

text.description: The Kon-Tiki Museum stands on the Bygdøy peninsula in Oslo and tells the story of Thor Heyerdahl's sea voyages. It was built to house the Kon-Tiki, the balsa-wood raft he sailed from Peru to Polynesia in 1947. Inside you will also find the reed boat Ra II, which he sailed from North Africa to the Caribbean, and a model of the whale shark the crew met on the Kon-Tiki voyage. The current building opened in 1957, and an extension followed in 1978. For the photo, treat the museum building as a straightforward record of the place: the entrance, the name and a bit of the surroundings. Bygdøy has several other museums nearby, including the Fram Museum, the Viking Ship Museum and the Norwegian Maritime Museum. Stand back far enough to fit the whole front in the frame, keep the phone level so the lines of the building stay straight, and take a second shot closer in on the entrance or signage. Check the official site before visiting.
text.geographic_location: On the Bygdøy peninsula in Oslo, in the group of museums near the Fram Museum, the Viking Ship Museum and the Norwegian Maritime Museum.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. The museum is on the Bygdøy peninsula in Oslo, among the other Bygdøy museums, so look for it near those. Once you are at the spot, the phone icon on the map is right at the museum itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole front of the building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough, and use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the entrance or signage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's edges with them so the walls stay upright. Take one wide shot of the whole front, then a closer one of the entrance. If you use the ultra-wide, keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the walls do not turn out too dark or the sky too pale.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime in good, even light is easiest for a clear shot of the building. Early or late in the day the light is softer, but check the museum's own times before planning around it.

text.access_note: Check the official site for opening times and any visitor rules before you go.

name: Fram Museum
label: Fram Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/128980495: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fram Museum' (77 m across).
notes: Polar ship Fram can be boarded inside the museum on Bygdøy.

text.description:
The Fram Museum sits on the Bygdøy peninsula and tells the story of Norwegian polar exploration. Its building is made around the polar ship Fram, which was designed and built by Colin Archer to Fridtjof Nansen's specifications and financed in 1891. The museum opened on 20 May 1936 and also honours Otto Sverdrup and Roald Amundsen. The museum also exhibits Gjøa, the first vessel to sail through the Northwest Passage, which Amundsen and a crew of six completed in 1906. Gjøa has its own dedicated building at the museum.

For a phone photographer the outside of the museum is the easy part. It is a large, distinctive building with a long outline, so it fills the frame well from a short way back. Stepping a few paces to the side and keeping the building's edges straight gives a tidy, balanced picture. Inside, the ship is much bigger than the space around it, so expect to use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in the hull and rigging. Visitors can go aboard Fram, and its original interior is intact, which gives you plenty of close-up details for the default lens (1x) or a little zoom. Other museums are close by, so you can easily build a photo walk around the peninsula. Rules on photography inside may vary, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: On the Bygdøy peninsula in Oslo, in a group of museums that includes the Kon-Tiki Museum, the Viking Ship Museum and the Norwegian Maritime Museum.
text.directions_text: The museum is on the Bygdøy peninsula in Oslo. Plan your own route to the peninsula. The museum is in the cluster of museums there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full building and for the ship inside. Use the default lens (1x) for general shots and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as rigging or signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. To photograph the building, walk to the outside of it and pick a spot with enough room to fit the long outline into the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the roof and walls with them so the building does not lean. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole front, then move closer with the default lens (1x) for a tighter, more detailed shot. Inside, shoot along the hull to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. Indoors, where light is low, hold the phone steady and let night mode work if it switches on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright but softly lit part of the day for the outside. For indoor shots, go whenever it is quietest so that other visitors are not in the frame.

text.access_note: Check the official site for opening times and ticket information before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Photography rules inside the museum may vary.
The building is large and distinctive enough to fill the frame from a short way back.
Inside the museum, the ship is large enough that an ultra-wide lens helps.
Other museums on Bygdøy are close enough to combine into a photo walk.
Quieter times of day mean fewer people in indoor photos.

name: Aker Brygge
label: Aker Brygge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tjuvholmen' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Tjuvholmen' (node/1424623689): point; moved 15 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1126488038: the OpenStreetMap point 'Aker brygge'.
notes: Waterfront district of restaurants and harbour views.

text.description:
Aker Brygge is Oslo's waterfront district, just west of the city centre on the Pipervika arm of the Oslofjord. Until 1982 it was the site of the Akers Mekaniske Verksted shipyard, and before 1854 the area was known as Holmen. Several of the big workshop halls were rebuilt as shops and restaurants, and the first stage of the new district was finished in 1986. Today it has a small boat harbour, a ferry terminal, apartments and offices, and it draws around 12 million visitors a year.

The best way to photograph it is from a little way off. From the pier at the Tjuvholmen end you look back at the whole waterfront, with the Astrup Fearnley museum pavilions in the foreground and the old city quarter beyond. That gives the view some depth, and it is usually calmer than the busy wharf itself. If you want the classic harbour scene instead, the Aker Brygge wharf shows the illuminated clock tower and wooden pier above still water, with evening crowds along the marina. For a higher, layered view of the harbour, the ramparts of Akershus Festning are a walk away.

Keep the horizon level with the gridlines on, and let the water fill the lower part of the frame so the reflections add to the picture. Wipe the lens before you start, as sea air and fingerprints soften evening shots.
text.geographic_location: Aker Brygge is in central Oslo, just west of downtown on the western side of Pipervika, next to the harbour. The Tjuvholmen pier is a short stroll south-west of it, near the Astrup Fearnley Museum of Modern Art.
text.directions_text: From the Aker Brygge waterfront, walk south-west along the water towards Tjuvholmen. Turn round at the end and look back to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the pavilions, the water and the waterfront together. Then try 2x to 3x to pick out the buildings and lights, or the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the foreground and sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Tjuvholmen (pier at the Tjuvholmen end, looking back east). Aker Brygge's waterfront seen from the Tjuvholmen side, with the Astrup Fearnley pavilions in the foreground and the old city quarter beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the pavilions low in the frame as a foreground anchor, with the Aker Brygge buildings and their reflections in the middle. Leave a band of sky above. For a different view, the Aker Brygge wharf shows the clock tower and the marina, and Akershus Festning gives a high, layered view with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon straight. Tap the waterfront lights to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so they don't glare. If your phone offers night mode in the dimmer light, let it run and hold still until it finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, the 30 minutes after sunset, when the lights come on and the sky still has some colour.

text.access_note: The pier and waterfront are free public spaces, but check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside any building or museum.
claims_not_in_sources: Resting your phone or elbows on a railing helps keep night shots steady.
Phones often switch to night mode automatically in dim light.
The Tjuvholmen pier is usually quieter than the main wharf in the evening.
Fingerprints and sea spray on the lens can soften photos.

name: Royal Palace
label: Royal Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Slottsplassen' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Slottsplassen' (relation/12806921): middle (270 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/12267199: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Royal Palace' (161 m across).
notes: The king's residence at the top of Karl Johans gate.

text.description: The Royal Palace is the official residence of the Norwegian monarch, and it closes the long view up Karl Johans gate. It was built in the first half of the 19th century for Charles XIV John, the French-born king of Norway and Sweden. The architect was Hans Linstow. The foundation stone was laid in 1825, the roof went on in 1836, and the interiors were finished in the late 1840s. The pale, calm facade, its central colonnade and its three storeys suit a phone camera well, because the building is simple and symmetrical and easy to straighten with gridlines. From the front forecourt, Slottsplassen, you get the full palace facade with the equestrian statue of Karl Johan in the foreground. This is the standard frontal composition, and the statue adds depth to the frame. One guide suggests standing a little to the left side of the forecourt rather than dead centre, which gives a slight angle and a less flat picture. The palace sits in the Palace Park (Slottsparken), a public park of about 22 hectares, so there is room to step back for a wider view. The changing of the guard happens daily at 1:30pm. If you want it in your photo, arrive about 10 minutes early to secure a good position. Photography is not allowed inside the palace.
text.geographic_location: The Royal Palace stands at the end of Karl Johans gate in central Oslo. It is surrounded by the Palace Park, with the Palace Square (Slottsplassen) in front.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the top of Karl Johans gate in central Oslo and head for the palace at the end of the street. Slottsplassen, the forecourt, is the recommended viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade with the statue. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand close and the building will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the colonnade or the balcony.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Slottsplassen (front forecourt, facing the palace facade). The full palace facade with the equestrian statue of Karl Johan in the foreground, the standard frontal composition. Try a spot slightly to the left side of the forecourt rather than straight on.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the palace's horizontal edges with them, so the building does not lean. Place the statue low in the frame to add depth, with the palace behind it. For a symmetrical alternative, Karl Johans gate shows the palace centred at the top of the avenue. Slottsparken gives the whole palace framed at the top of a tree-lined avenue, from a short distance away.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the pale facade keeps its detail. Take a few shots in case people walk into the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check on the day: the facade may look best in the morning from Slottsplassen, or afternoon sun may light it better. Try both if you can. For the changing of the guard at 1:30pm daily, arrive about 10 minutes early.

text.access_note: The grounds are free and open to the public, but photography is not allowed inside the palace, so check the official site before you go for tours and any current closures or rules.

name: Karl Johans gate
label: Karl Johans gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Stortinget' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Stortinget' (way/29132806): middle (121 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Main promenade from the station to the Royal Palace.

text.description: Karl Johans gate is the main street of Oslo, and it photographs best as one long straight view. It runs uphill from the Parliament building (Stortinget) to the yellow Royal Palace, and the wide avenue, the palace at the top and the open sky above make a simple, balanced frame. The western part of the street was built in the 1840s to link the newly built palace with the rest of the city. It was named Karl Johans gate in 1852, after the recently deceased King Charles III John, who was also King Charles XIV John of Sweden. When the Parliament building was finished in 1866, two formerly separate streets were joined and the whole length took the name. An equestrian statue of the king stands in front of the palace, added in 1875. Guides point to the front plaza of Stortinget as one of the best places to shoot the avenue, and it is also a natural spot to pause out of the flow of people. From there, the palace sits at the top of the street and catches the morning sun on its facade. If you want a higher, wider view, Slottsparken gives an elevated look back down the street. Studenterlunden, beside the National Theatre, gives a closer frame with trees and the busy avenue. The street is also the main route for Norway's Constitution Day celebrations on 17 May, so it can look very different on that day.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Oslo, running between the Parliament building (Stortinget) and the Royal Palace at Slottsplassen. The street passes the National Theatre and its greenery along the way.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Parliament building (Stortinget) in central Oslo, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further out. The street itself is a very short stroll east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full view of the avenue and palace. Try the telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the palace closer and make the street look more compact. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the plaza and buildings around you in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Stortinget (front plaza, facing the Royal Palace up the avenue). Karl Johans gate running uphill from the Parliament toward the yellow Royal Palace, with the morning sun lighting the palace facade. The street on the map is a short step to the east, behind you as you face the palace. From here the photo shows Karl Johans gate rising from the Parliament towards the yellow palace.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the middle of the avenue on the central vertical line so the street leads the eye up to the palace. Hold the phone level, because the strong lines of the buildings make a tilt obvious. For a different angle, Slottsparken gives a higher view back down the street, and Studenterlunden gives a closer, greener frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the facade keeps its colour. Wait a moment for people to cross the frame, or take a Live Photo and pick the cleanest moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sun lights the front of the palace.

text.access_note: Karl Johans gate and the plaza in front of Stortinget are open public space, but on 17 May and during Christmas market periods access and the look of the street can change, so check the official site before you go if you are visiting then.

name: National Museum of Norway
label: National Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1132918: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Norway's largest art museum, near the harbour.

text.description: The National Museum (Nasjonalmuseet) is Norway's state collection of art, architecture and design. It opened in June 2022 in a new building on the site of the old Oslo West Station, at Vestbanen on the edge of Aker Brygge. The collection runs to over 400,000 works, including the first copy of Edvard Munch's The Scream from 1893. The building is a large, calm block of pale stone and dark metal, and it photographs well because of its clean lines and plain surfaces. The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so start there, then step out to the harbour-side approach and back away from the building. Once you have some distance, the Light Hall's granite and brick facade can fit in the frame, with the harbour around you. Walk a few steps along the front for a second angle. For a more formal shot, a symmetrical view of the bronze-and-glass front lets the metal panels pick up the colour of the sky. Look out for the view toward Aker Brygge too. It makes a good contrasting shot, with the modern waterfront buildings beside the museum's heavy stone. Exterior photos are not affected by the museum's rules, but check for photography restrictions inside before you take your phone into the galleries.
text.geographic_location: In central Oslo, in the former Oslo West Station building at Vestbanen, on the harbour edge beside Aker Brygge. The address is Brynjulf Bulls plass 3.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Aker Brygge, which is right next to the museum, and walk towards the harbour side of the building. The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so there is no further walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are standing close and the building will not fit. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the granite, brick and metal panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Then step out to the harbour-side approach and back away from the building, so the Light Hall's granite and brick facade fits in the frame and you can see it properly from outside.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so the walls do not lean. Hold the phone level and step back far enough to keep the whole front in the frame. For an alternative, move to the centre of the front for a symmetrical view of the bronze-and-glass facade, with the metal panels reflecting the sky. Turn towards Aker Brygge for a second, wider shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. Keep the phone level in portrait or landscape and avoid tilting it upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight suits the stone and metal best. Overcast skies give even, calm colours, and low sun can add warmth. Try both a wide shot and a close shot whatever the light.

text.access_note: The outside and the waterfront approach are open public space, but entry to the galleries and any rules for photography inside may vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft or overcast daylight suits pale stone and metal facades, and low sun can add warmth.
Aker Brygge is right next to the museum and can be used as a starting point for walking.
Keeping the phone level and using gridlines helps keep vertical building edges straight.

name: Oslo City Hall
label: Oslo City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rådhusplassen' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rådhusplassen' (way/1062404152): middle (261 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24900009: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Oslo City Hall' (135 m across).
notes: Brick twin-tower building where the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded.

text.description: Oslo City Hall (Oslo rådhus) is a big red-brick building on the waterfront, topped by two towers of different heights, 63 and 66 metres. It was built between 1931 and 1950, with a pause during the Second World War, and was designed by Arnstein Arneberg and Magnus Poulsson. The bricks are larger than was usual in the 1930s, closer to medieval brick, and that gives the walls a chunky, textured look that shows up well on a phone screen. It photographs well because the plain, strong shapes of the facade and towers sit against open sky, and there is a lot of detail to pick out. Colourful reliefs by Dagfin Werenskiold on the square side show scenes from the Poetic Edda, and sculptures stand in front of the building. The City Hall also hosts the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony every 10 December, so expect crowds and possible closures around then. The best all-round view is from the open square in front of the main facade, where you can step back far enough to get both towers in. If you would rather have a harbour scene, Rådhusbryggene shows the towers across the water with ferries and boats in the foreground. The building is closed on some days for official events, so check the official site before you go if you plan to see inside.
text.geographic_location: Oslo City Hall is in the city centre, in the northern part of the Pipervika neighbourhood, facing the Oslofjord. The open square, Rådhusplassen, lies in front of the main facade.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the city centre and the Pipervika waterfront on foot or by whatever local transport you prefer. Once there, make for the open square in front of the City Hall. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and both towers into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the reliefs, the sculptures and the tops of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rådhusplassen (the open square in front of the main facade). A wide-angle view of the civic facade and towers across the open square. From here the building lies to the north-east, and you get a wide view of the civic facade and towers across the open space.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a tower up with a vertical grid line so the walls stay upright. Keep your phone level, as tilting it back makes the towers lean. Use the ultra-wide for the full facade, then move closer and use the telephoto for a Werenskiold relief. For a different view, Rådhusbryggene on the harbour frames the towers with boats and ferries in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the red brick keeps its colour and the sky isn't washed out. If people walk through the square, take a short burst or a Live Photo and choose the cleanest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people, and the brick looks warmer in low sun. Avoid 10 December if you want a quiet square.

text.access_note: The square in front is open public space, but the City Hall is closed on some days for official events and photography is restricted during ceremonies, so check the official site before you go.

name: Storting Building
label: Storting (Parliament)
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Eidsvolls plass' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Eidsvolls plass' (way/841080897): middle (128 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q6515317: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The Norwegian Parliament building on Karl Johans gate.

text.description:
The Storting building is Norway's parliament, a broad yellow-brick building on Karl Johans gate in central Oslo. Its most distinctive feature is the curved central section at the front. This holds the main debating chamber, rather than placing it in the middle of the building. The pale grey granite base and the yellow walls give a calm, even colour that phones handle well. It was designed by the Swedish architect Emil Victor Langlet and taken into use on 5 March 1866. The two stone lions on the sloping approach, known as Løvebakken (the Lions Hill), have stood there since 1865. They add a lower, closer subject to your photos.

The open forecourt of Eidsvolls plass, directly in front, is the best place to read the building's curves and proportions. From here you get a clear head-on view of the whole façade with space around it. For a second picture, walk up towards the lions and shoot low, with the entrance and façade rising behind them. Stortingsparken gives a softer view across the greenery, and it is a good spot if you are there near sunset. Stay outside for your photos, as indoor photography is restricted in working parliamentary areas. Keep your phone level so the long horizontal lines stay straight.
text.geographic_location: The Storting building stands at Karl Johans gate 22 in central Oslo. Eidsvolls plass is the open square in front of it, and Stortingsparken is close by.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot. Start from the Karl Johans gate area in central Oslo and walk towards the Storting building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full façade from the square. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and ground, and watch the edges for stretching. Use 2x or 3x telephoto for the lions and the curved central section.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Eidsvolls plass (front forecourt, facing the main façade). The full yellow-brick façade and its curved central assembly hall, framed by the open square in front. From here the building lies to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up so its base sits on a horizontal line. Keep the curved central section near the middle of the frame. For a different view, go to Løvebakken and shoot low, with a lion in the foreground and the entrance behind. Stortingsparken is another option, for the building across the green space.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the yellow brick keeps its colour. Use portrait mode only for the lion close-ups.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the brickwork than harsh midday sun. Near sunset, Stortingsparken gives a good view of the building with a colourful sky.

text.access_note: The square, park and lion steps are outdoor public spaces, but check the official site before you go for tours, public gallery access and any restrictions inside.

name: Oslo Cathedral
label: Oslo Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Stortorvet' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Stortorvet' (way/179095465): middle (110 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/33204291: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Oslo Cathedral' (78 m across).
notes: Baroque church in the city centre with a painted ceiling.

text.description:
Oslo Cathedral is the main church of the Church of Norway's Oslo diocese and the parish church for the city centre. It is the third cathedral in Oslo's history. The present building went up between 1694 and 1697, and it was consecrated in November 1697. It was rebuilt between 1848 and 1850, restored for the city's 900th anniversary in 1950, and reopened in April 2010 after a long renovation. Royal weddings have been held here, including Prince Haakon's in 2001.

It photographs well because the tower gives a strong vertical line, and the square in front gives you room to step back. The classic view is from Stortorvet, across the street from the main facade. A statue of Christian IV is reported in the foreground, looking up at the church. If it is still there, your picture has a clear front, middle and background, so check it is in place when you arrive. The lower end of the cathedral is wrapped by the curved Bazaar buildings and the old Fire Watch, both built between 1840 and 1859. They are worth a second frame if you walk round.

The carillon inside the tower now marks the hours and quarter-hours, so you may hear it while you shoot. Take a few frames from slightly different spots in the square. Keep the tower upright by holding the phone level, and use the gridlines to help. If you have time, try the street-level view from Karl Johans gate too.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Oslo, at Stortorvet square, just north/north-east of Karl Johans gate and between Kirke gate and Dronningens gate. The Bazaar buildings wrap around the lower end of the church.
text.directions_text: Make for Karl Johans gate in the city centre, as Stortorvet lies just to the north/north-east of it. By taxi or hired scooter, ask for Oslo Cathedral (Oslo domkirke) and get out at Stortorvet. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the tower and facade, and the statue if it is there, sit together in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole tower and a lot of foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower top and its details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Stortorvet (across the street from the cathedral's main facade). The cathedral's bronze-steepled tower and pale yellow brick facade, with the Christian IV statue in the foreground looking up at the church. The cathedral is to the east. A statue of Christian IV is reported in the foreground, looking up at the church, so check it is still in place when you arrive.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and, if the statue is there, place it low in the frame with the tower rising behind it. Keep the phone level and upright so the tower does not lean. For a different look, try Karl Johans gate for the full street-level facade and clock tower, or Eidsvolls plass for the tower above greenery in a quieter setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the details in the facade are not washed out. If a person walks into the frame, try a Live Photo and pick the cleanest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon light suits the street-level view from Karl Johans gate.

text.access_note: Stortorvet is a free viewpoint, but the cathedral is a working church used for services and events, so check the official site before you go if you want to photograph inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The statue of Christian IV at Stortorvet is reported by a single blog, so it should be checked on site.

name: Norwegian Museum of Cultural History
label: Norwegian Folk Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gol Stavkirke' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Gol stavkirke' (way/161661199): middle (21 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/134403996: large area 'The Norwegian Museum of Cultural History' (693 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Open-air museum with a stave church on Bygdøy.

text.description: The Norwegian Museum of Cultural History (Norsk Folkemuseum) sits on the Bygdøy peninsula. It has extensive collections and also a large open-air museum with more than 150 buildings brought here from towns and country districts across Norway. For photographs, the best-known building is the Gol stave church. Its dark tarred timber walls, steep layered roofs and carved portal stand out well against the green grounds. The church dates from the 13th century and joined the museum in 1907. It is one of five medieval buildings on site, and part of a group of relocated buildings that is recognised as the world's first open-air museum. You can walk right round the outside, so you get several different angles. The carvings tend to look best in open shade outside rather than in the dim interior. If you want a contrast, the old-town area has a three-storey brick townhouse from Wessels gate 15, built in 1865 and moved here from Oslo. It shows well among the neighbouring old-town buildings. The museum was founded in 1894 and opened to the public in 1901, so the grounds have had a long time to settle into their setting. Take a slow lap of the church before you start, and look for the portal and the roof lines. Phone photos work well here because the subjects are close and the shapes are strong. Check the museum's official site before you go, as some outdoor buildings may be closed or viewable only from outside in winter.
text.geographic_location: On the Bygdøy peninsula in western Oslo, in the area of museums that includes the Viking Ship Museum, the Fram Museum and the Kon-Tiki Museum.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot. The museum is on the Bygdøy peninsula, so look for the Norwegian Museum of Cultural History there. From there the middle of the museum is to the south-east, about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole church. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the walls and want the full height of the roofs. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved portal and the wooden details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (outside the church, walking around the tarred walls and the carved portal). The tarred timber stave church with its dark walls, steep roofs and carved details, set against the museum's green grounds. The wider museum grounds lie to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the church off-centre with the green grounds around it. Move round the building to try several angles, and finish with a close shot of the portal carvings. If you walk on into the old-town area, a framed shot of the Wessels gate 15 brick townhouse makes a good second picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: The tarred walls are very dark, so tap on the wall to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky starts to wash out. Keep the phone steady against your body for close carving shots, and do not rely on a tripod, as these may be restricted inside the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light works best, according to one guide.

text.access_note: Some outdoor buildings may be closed or viewable only from outside in winter, so check the museum's official site before you go.

name: Nobel Peace Center
label: Nobel Peace Center
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rådhusplassen' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rådhusplassen' (way/1062404152): middle (261 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/8046314379: the OpenStreetMap point 'Nobel Peace Center'.
notes: Museum in the old Vestbanen station by the harbour.

text.description:
The Nobel Peace Center is a museum about the Nobel Peace Prize, housed in a handsome yellow building that began life as a railway station. Architect Georg Andreas Bull drew the former Vestbanestasjon (West station) in 1872, and trains stopped using it in 1989. The centre opened in 2005 and is now one of Norway's most visited museums, with around 250,000 visitors a year. It sits on the City Hall Square beside the harbour, a short walk from Oslo City Hall, where the Peace Prize ceremony takes place every 10 December.

It photographs well because you can see the whole building across open ground, with the fjord and City Hall in the same sequence as you walk across the square. A good plan is to walk across the square and take a few frames as the scene changes, rather than one shot from a single spot. If you want a closer look at the entrance, Brynjulf Bulls plass in front of the building gives the most direct view of the facade. Rådhusbryggene, by the water, gives a quieter angle with the harbour and civic buildings beside it. Keep your phone level and use gridlines so the long front doesn't lean.
text.geographic_location: In central Oslo, on the City Hall Square (Rådhusplassen) beside the harbour, close to Oslo City Hall. It occupies the old West railway station building.
text.directions_text: Start from Oslo City Hall, the well-known landmark next to the square, or from the City Hall Square itself, and walk from there. Walk west across the plaza towards the yellow building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building across the plaza. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and the fjord in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rådhusplassen (plaza end nearest the Nobel Peace Center, with City Hall behind the frame). The yellow former railway station seen across the City Hall plaza, with the fjord and City Hall in the same sequence.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the horizontal lines so the long front stays straight. Leave some sky and a strip of the plaza so the building has room. For a different angle, try Brynjulf Bulls plass for a straight-on shot of the entrance, or Rådhusbryggene for the harbour beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the yellow walls keep their colour. In the evening, try night mode but hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening is a good choice, as the plaza is likely to be quieter then.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but the museum inside charges admission and temporary exhibitions may restrict photography, so check the official site before you go.

name: Holmenkollbakken
label: Holmenkollen Ski Jump
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kongeveien' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Kongeveien nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/173145217: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Holmenkollbakken' (208 m across).
notes: Famous ski jump on the hill above the city.

text.description:
Holmenkollbakken is Oslo's famous ski jump, a huge ski jump with a steel tower that stands out above the forest at Holmenkollen. The hill is rated HS134, can hold 70,000 spectators and has hosted the 1952 Winter Olympics and several Nordic World Ski Championships. Skiing events have been held here since 1892, and the whole structure was torn down and rebuilt between 2008 and 2010, so what you see today is a modern jump on a very old site.

It photographs well because of its shape. The long, steep run and the tall tower give you strong diagonal lines, and the dark trees around it make the pale structure easy to pick out. The suggested place to get the whole thing in one picture is Kongeveien, on the stretch past the run-out end of the jump. From there you should see the full length of the jump from its lower end, with the steel tower rising above the trees. It is a public road, so it costs nothing and needs no ticket.

If you have time for a second picture, Holmenkollen kapell, the small wooden chapel in the forest, has the jump behind it as a backdrop. You can also walk to the base for a close, steep view up the lower slope. The top-of-tower platform is mainly a city-view spot rather than a place to photograph the jump itself.
text.geographic_location: Holmenkollbakken is at Holmenkollen, in the wooded hills above Oslo. It is part of the Holmenkollen National Arena, which also has the smaller Midtstubakken hill and cross-country and biathlon venues.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Holmenkollen area. The stretch of Kongeveien past the run-out end of the jump is the suggested viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because you are close and the jump is long and tall. Switch to the default lens (1x) if you can step back far enough to fit it all in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter picture of the tower against the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kongeveien (stretch past the run-out end of the jump, on the main road back toward the metro). The whole length of the jump from its lower end, with the steel tower rising above the trees. At that distance you are very close, so expect to shoot upwards and may not fit the whole length in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and hold the phone upright so the tower stands straight. Let the slope run diagonally through the frame, with the tower at the top. If you are on the road, keep its edge low down so the jump stays the main subject. For a different picture, try the chapel with the jump behind it, or walk to the base and shoot steeply upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale sky does not wash out the steel. Take a few shots, because walkers or vehicles on the road may pass through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day, or on a bright overcast day, helps the steel and trees show clearly without harsh shadows.

text.access_note: Kongeveien is an open public road with no ticket needed, but the area can be closed or restricted during competitions and events, so check the official site before you go.

label: Astrup Fearnley

notes: Renzo Piano's modern art museum on Tjuvholmen.

text.description:
The Astrup Fearnley Museum sits on the tip of Tjuvholmen, and its sail-shaped glass roof is what you notice first. Seen from the water's edge, the roof stands out against the fjord, which makes the building an easy landmark to photograph. It is also a good way to place yourself in the city, because the Aker Brygge waterfront and Oslo City Hall sit behind it in the same frame.

The phone icon on the map is right at the museum on the Tjuvholmen tip, where you can photograph the sweep of the roof up close. For a wider view, go to Strandpromenaden, the harbour promenade on the fjord side, and look back at the museum. From there the curved roof is the main subject. Oslo City Hall and the Aker Brygge buildings give the picture depth and show where you are. A second option is Tjuvholmen Sculpture Park, where the outdoor sculptures can frame the museum, with the fjord and, across the bay, Akershus Fortress behind.

For a simple picture, keep the roof's sweeping line in the upper half of the frame and let the water fill the lower part. If you want people in the shot for scale, wait until a few walkers pass along the promenade. The museum itself charges admission. The rooftop terrace and glass bridge are inside the building, so this guide sticks to the views from outside. If you want to take photos indoors, check the museum's photography policy first.
text.geographic_location: On the tip of Tjuvholmen in central Oslo, with the Aker Brygge waterfront nearby. Oslo City Hall is visible across the harbour behind the museum.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot. The museum stands on the Tjuvholmen tip, beside the Aker Brygge waterfront, so head for the tip of Tjuvholmen. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole roof with the waterfront and City Hall behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the roof will not fit. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the roof's lines against City Hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the sail-shaped glass roof is the main subject. For the wider view, try Strandpromenaden, the harbour promenade on the fjord side facing the museum, where the roof sits in front of the Aker Brygge waterfront and Oslo City Hall. Tjuvholmen Sculpture Park is another option, putting sculptures in front of the museum, with the fjord and Akershus Fortress behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the roof on one of the upper lines, with the fjord taking up the lower third. Keep the horizon level so the buildings across the water do not lean. For a variation, try the sculpture park viewpoint and use a nearby sculpture as a foreground frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the roof to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the glass keeps its detail. A Live Photo can catch walkers or boats passing, and you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the light is soft, such as morning or later in the afternoon, and check the weather. Glass and water both reflect a lot, so a very bright midday sun can wash out the picture.

text.access_note: The promenade is a public street, but the museum itself charges admission, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: National Theatre
label: National Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Johanne Dybwads plass' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Johanne Dybwads plass' (relation/3576237): middle (81 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4368869: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Theatre' (105 m across).
notes: Historic theatre with statues of Ibsen and Bjørnson in front.

text.description:
The National Theatre (Nationaltheatret) is one of Norway's largest and most prominent venues for the dramatic arts, and its neo-baroque front is the part to photograph. From the open square in front of it you can see the whole facade, with the statues of the playwrights Ibsen and Bjørnson flanking the entrance. That gives you a tidy, balanced picture with a clear subject.

The theatre gave its first performance on 1 September 1899, though its roots go back to the Christiania Theatre, founded in 1829. The opening programme included Ibsen's An Enemy of the People and Bjørnson's Sigurd Jorsalfar. The building was designed by the architect Henrik Bull and stands between the Royal Palace and the Parliament, so it is easy to fit into a walk around the centre. The theatre is often thought of as the home of Ibsen's plays, which is why his statue matters to the picture.

For a phone, the square works well because you can step back far enough to fit the whole front in. Put the statues in the foreground to give a sense of scale, and keep the building straight in the frame. If you want a different view, try Studenterlunden or Stortingsparken, where trees soften the foreground. The exterior is the practical subject here, as photography inside is generally restricted during performances.
text.geographic_location: In central Oslo, on the square in front of the National Theatre, between the Royal Palace and the Parliament of Norway.
text.directions_text: Head for the National Theatre in the centre of Oslo, between the Royal Palace and the Parliament. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close shot of one statue or the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Johanne Dybwads plass (in front of the main facade, between the Ibsen and Bjørnson statues). The neo-baroque front of the National Theatre with both playwright statues flanking the entrance, framed by the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the central entrance with the middle of the frame so the building looks straight. Include one statue at the edge as a foreground frame. If you want a change, Studenterlunden and Stortingsparken both give a softer view with trees in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few shots in case people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the low western sun lights the stone facade and statues. Flat, overcast midday light makes the statues look duller.

text.access_note: The square in front of the theatre is open public space; check the official site before you go if you want to see inside, as interior photography is generally restricted during performances.
